GharaoteriBtiOB. — Passiflora has not been proved. Its curative
action appears to be of a direct kind. Hale introduced it to homceo-
pathy, citing in the New Remedies a paper by L. Phares. Phares
learned its action from W. B. Lindsay, who used it with extraordinary
success in tetanus of the newborn. Án aqueous extract of the root
Lindsay commended as an application f or cnancre, erysipelas, irritable
piles, and new bums. Phares conñrms the efficacy of Passif, in
erysipelas (he "never saw anything act so promptly"), ulcers,
neuralgia, and tetanus. He cites the case of an oíd lady who was
seized with convulsions of a tetanic nature, and refers to several cases
of tetanus in the horse cured by himself and his son, J. H. Phares.
One of his own horses was seized with tetanus, and all hope of saving
him was given up, when Phares gathered some Passif. — stems,
leaves, and fiowers — ^pounded, moistened with water, expressed ten or
twelve ounces, and poured it dowh the animal's throat throngh a
tubc introduced at the side of his mouth. Though not expected to
Uve h^ an hour, the horse was found grazing next moming. Far-
rington considers Passif. suited especially to tetanus of hot countries,
and refers to two cures by Archibald Bavne of Barbados with the f
and i X. It has also been used in convulsions of children and other
complaints of dentition, and even in epilepsy. J. W. Covert (Hom.

Passif, has been also used for ordinary sleeplessness ; for restlessness
